Title: ANTHROPOLOGY (ANTH) < University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill
Chunks: 6,7,8
Evolutionary and ecological approach to understanding the human species' past and contemporary human variation. Emphasis on evolutionary processes, biological adaptation, and biocultural interactions with diverse environments.
**Rules & Requirements**
**Grading Status:**Letter grade.
**ANTH 144.****Archaeology and the Media.****3 Credits.**
This class will examine how archaeology is represented in the media. This will include the characterization of archaeology and archaeologists in film and written fiction. This course will also examine the dissemination of archaeological findings through fact based presentations such as television documentaries and material published for the general public's consumption.
**Rules & Requirements**
**Grading Status:**Letter grade.
**ANTH 145.****Introduction to World Prehistory.****3 Credits.**
Introduction to world prehistory and archaeological methods. Examines the development of human society from the emergence of modern human beings 100,000 years ago through the formation of ancient civilizations.
**Rules & Requirements**
**IDEAs in Action Gen Ed:**FC-GLOBAL or FC-PAST.
**Grading Status:**Letter grade.
**ANTH 147.****Comparative Healing Systems.****3 Credits.**
In this course we compare a variety of healing beliefs and practices so that students may gain a better understanding of their own society, culture, and medical system.
**Rules & Requirements**
**IDEAs in Action Gen Ed:**FC-GLOBAL or FC-KNOWING.
**Grading Status:**Letter grade.
**ANTH 148.****Human Origins.****3 Credits.**
Study of human evolution. Focus on the fossil record of humans and human-like ancestors. Topics include communication, aggression, dietary adaptations, locomotion, major anatomical changes, and behavioral shifts in an evolutionary framework.
**Rules & Requirements**
**IDEAs in Action Gen Ed:**FC-NATSCI.
**Grading Status:**Letter grade.
**ANTH 149.****Great Discoveries in Archaeology.****3 Credits.**
This course provides students with a detailed look at some of the most significant archaeological discoveries from around the world, including Neanderthals, Stonehenge, and the Egyptian pyramids.
**Rules & Requirements**
**IDEAs in Action Gen Ed:**FC-GLOBAL or FC-PAST.
**Grading Status:**Letter grade.

**ANTH 151.****Anthropological Perspectives on Food and Culture.****3 Credits.**
Anthropological perspectives on foodways. This course examines the biological basis of human diets as well as the historical and cultural contexts of food production, preparation, presentation, and consumption.
**Rules & Requirements**
**IDEAs in Action Gen Ed:**FC-GLOBAL or FC-PAST.
**Grading Status:**Letter grade.
**ANTH 190.****Special Topics in Anthropology I.****1-4 Credits.**
Examines selected topics from an anthropological perspective. Course description is available from the departmental office.
**Rules & Requirements**
**Repeat Rules:**May be repeated for credit; may be repeated in the same term for different topics; 8 total credits. 2 total completions.
**Grading Status:**Letter grade.
**ANTH 194.****Anthropology and Community Development.****3 Credits.**
The course examines ethnographic, theoretical, practical, and policy approaches to community development and community organizations in America and the English-speaking Caribbean. Students can work with a local community organization.
**Rules & Requirements**
**IDEAs in Action Gen Ed:**FC-KNOWING or FC-VALUES.
**Grading Status:**Letter grade.
**ANTH 195.****Research in Anthropology I.****1-3 Credits.**
Permission of the instructor. Data collection, analysis, and interpretation for independent research project.
**Rules & Requirements**
**Repeat Rules:**May be repeated for credit. 6 total credits. 2 total completions.
**Grading Status:**Letter grade.
**ANTH 196.****Independent Reading or Study in Anthropology I.****1-3 Credits.**
Permission of the instructor. Reading and study under a faculty member whose interests coincide with those of the individual student.
**Rules & Requirements**
**Repeat Rules:**May be repeated for credit. 12 total credits. 4 total completions.
**Grading Status:**Letter grade.
**ANTH 198H.****First Year Honors in Anthropology II.****3 Credits.**
Open to honors candidates. Permission of the instructor is required. Reading or study under a faculty member whose interests coincide with those of the individual student.
**Rules & Requirements**
**Grading Status:**Letter grade.

**ANTH 202.****Everyday Cultures: Folklore in America.****3 Credits.**
An introduction to the study of creativity and aesthetic expression in everyday life, considering both traditional genres and contemporary innovations in the material, verbal, and musical arts.
**Rules & Requirements**
**IDEAs in Action Gen Ed:**FC-AESTH or FC-KNOWING.
**Grading Status:**Letter grade.
**ANTH 203.****Approaches to American Indian Studies.****3 Credits.**
Introduces students to the disciplines comprising American Indian studies and teaches them how to integrate disciplines for a more complete understanding of the experiences of American Indian peoples.
**Rules & Requirements**
**IDEAs in Action Gen Ed:**FC-KNOWING or FC-POWER.
**Grading Status:**Letter grade.
**ANTH 204.****From Ayahuasca to Zoloft: Anthropological Approaches to Drugs and Drug Use.****3 Credits.**
This course considers the cultural, social, political, medical, and biological aspects of drugs (legal, illegal, pharmaceutical, botanical, and otherwise) through space and time. We take an interdisciplinary approach drawing on research from anthropology, science studies, biology, history, ethnobotany, and sociology to examine what counts as a drug, who determines what is a drug, why people use drugs, and how drugs influence us as individuals and as a society.
**Rules & Requirements**
**IDEAs in Action Gen Ed:**FC-GLOBAL, RESEARCH.
**Grading Status:**Letter grade.
**ANTH 206.****American Indian Societies.****3 Credits.**
Explores the tremendous diversity that exists within and across American Indian nations, together with the concerns, issues, and challenges that shape the futures American Indians are charting for themselves.
**Rules & Requirements**
**Grading Status:**Letter grade.
**ANTH 210I.****Global Issues and Globalization.****3 Credits.**
Survey of international social, political, and cultural patterns in selected societies of Africa, Asia, America, and Europe, stressing comparative analysis of conflicts and change in different historical contexts. LAC recitation sections offered in French, German, and Spanish.
**Rules & Requirements**
**IDEAs in Action Gen Ed:**FC-GLOBAL or FC-POWER, INTERDISCI.
**Grading Status:**Letter grade.

Title: Medical Anthropology Major, B.A. < University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill
Chunks: 0,1,2,3,4
Medical anthropology addresses the biological, cultural, and political-economic dimensions of health, illness, and healing historically and at present. Reflecting the multi-disciplinary character of its parent field of anthropology, medical anthropology deploys quantitative and qualitative methods to examine the body as a site of evolutionary processes and cultural symbols. Medical anthropology considers healing as a set of interpretive processes occurring at multiple, complex levels.
This program provides students with the fundamental knowledge and exposure needed to pursue careers and post-graduate studies in fields related to global health, public health, allied health care, health and human services, health policy, medicine, dentistry, and other emerging disciplines.
For students seeking a career in the health professions, the program in medical anthropology complements training in the natural sciences. Courses in medical anthropology explore population variations in health outcomes due to the influence of environment, context, and culture. The curriculum also equips students with ways to understand the meanings people find in illness and healing as well as the moral stakes of medical decisions. Additionally, courses in medical anthropology give students awareness of the formal institutions and social relations that become the channels and limitations of technical knowledge about illness and healing.

## Student Learning Outcomes
Upon completion of the medical anthropology program, students should be able to:
*   Demonstrate knowledge of the relationships between humans' health and historical, biocultural, and societal dynamics  
*   Demonstrate understanding of the ways comparative cultural and historical experiences impact health-related values and practices, definitions of illness, and methods of healing  
*   Demonstrate competence in reading, analyzing, and communicating social science research on health  
*   Gain experience conducting and/or applying research using medical anthropology's methods  
*   Gain an understanding of medical anthropology's relationships to the holistic, parent discipline of anthropology and its contributions to applied professional fields such as medicine and global health.

## Requirements
In addition to the program requirements, students must
*   earn a minimum final cumulative GPA of 2.000  
*   complete a minimum of 45 academic credit hours earned from UNC–Chapel Hill courses  
*   take at least half of their major core requirements (courses and credit hours) at UNC–Chapel Hill  
*   earn a minimum cumulative GPA of 2.000 in the major core requirements. Some programs may require higher standards for major or specific courses.
For more information, please consult the degree requirements section of the catalog.

Anthropology is the integrative study of human beings at all times and in all places. Anthropological expertise has special application for hidden histories and the ancient past; the intersection of human biology and ecology; and the way communities create and use meaning, values, and history in everyday life. Students interested in choosing anthropology as a major or minor should visit the department’s website and click on the link for the undergraduate program. Students planning a major in anthropology should contact the department’s Director of Undergraduate Studies with any questions or concerns. Majors may consult with the Director of Undergraduate Studies on a regular basis for assistance or information about their path through the program.

## Student Learning Outcomes
Upon completion of the anthropology program, students should be able to:
*   Discuss and critically assess theories and concepts for the study of social, cultural, and biological forms, phenomena, and change in the human species  
*   Engage in the coherent, holistic, integrative study of humans over time and space

*   Demonstrate an in-depth knowledge of human social, cultural, and biological heterogeneity, within a framework that affirms the essential unity of the human species

## Requirements

*   earn a minimum final cumulative GPA of 2.000  
*   complete a minimum of 45 academic credit hours earned from UNC–Chapel Hill courses  
*   take at least half of their major core requirements (courses and credit hours) at UNC–Chapel Hill  
*   earn a minimum cumulative GPA of 2.000 in the major core requirements. Some programs may require higher standards for major or specific courses.

## Special Opportunities in Anthropology
### Honors in Anthropology
Writing an honors thesis is an excellent way to cap one’s major in anthropology. The process offers students the chance to carry out original research on a topic that they are passionate about. Our thesis writers work closely with a faculty advisor and committee members to develop their project during their junior year. The department provides support, offering a specific seminar during the fall (ANTH 691H) and a corresponding independent study or seminar course (ANTH 692H), that together walk students through the essential steps of writing up their research. For our students, writing an honors thesis continues to prove a pivotal experience—at once a capstone to their studies at Carolina and an achievement to carry with them into their lives and careers beyond.
To pursue an honors thesis project, students must:
*   Be majoring in one of the department's majors.  
*   Maintain a minimum grade point average of 3.3 from the spring semester of the junior year through the entirety of the senior year.  
*   Secure a primary faculty advisor from the department during the junior year.  
*   Successfully complete the ANTH 691H and ANTH 692H sequence.  
*   Successfully complete any other research methods requirement as offered by the department for that honors cohort. See the Director of Undergraduate Studies for questions about this requirement.  
*   Receive approval from UNC’s Office for Human Research Ethics prior to the start of research, for all projects involving human subjects.

## Special Opportunities in Anthropology
### Honors in Anthropology
*   Students considering an honors thesis should first contact the honors thesis seminar instructor or the Director of Undergraduate Studies, during their junior year (or earlier).  
*   Eligible students next should secure an advisor prior to enrolling in ANTH 691H for the fall semester of their senior year. Typically, the advisor is a professor that they have worked with in a class or faculty member with shared interests.  
*   The bulk of data gathering should occur in the spring and summer after the junior year unless the student is working on an existing data set.  
*   In the fall students develop their research, analyze their data, and begin to write their thesis ANTH 691H.Students also form their committee, by adding two additional faculty members.  
*   In the spring, students complete an independent study with their advisor, focusing on writing the thesis ANTH 692Hor take ANTH 692H as a seminar (if offered).  
*   To complete the process, students defend (i.e., present and discuss) their thesis to their committee during the spring semester of the senior year.

## Special Opportunities in Anthropology
### Internships, Field Work, and Independent Study
Students who wish to explore an anthropological concern outside the conventional classroom setting, or who desire advanced or specialized work beyond current course offerings, should consider ANTH 393, ANTH 395, ANTH 396, ANTH 451, and ANTH 453.
ANTH 393 provides anthropology students the opportunity to engage in internships or other field experiences within or beyond the University that have a significant anthropological learning component. Variable credit may be obtained for this course. ANTH 393 is a controlled enrollment course; it requires the permission in advance of the faculty member sponsoring the internship, of a responsible official of the agency in which the internship is carried, and of the director of undergraduate studies. It is required that students make arrangements and secure permissions prior to the semester of the internship.
ANTH 396 provides anthropology students the opportunity to engage in independent study, and ANTH 395, the opportunity to engage in field research, in both cases under the mentoring of a specific faculty member. Variable credit may be obtained for these courses, although three units are usually expected. ANTH 396 and ANTH 395 require the permission of the faculty member under whom the student wishes to conduct research prior to the semester in which ANTH 396 or ANTH 395 is taken. Both are controlled enrollment courses. In general, these courses should be taken only by students with some prior coursework in anthropology or a related social science.
If interested in any of these independent study, independent research, or mentored internship credits, students should approach the faculty member they would like to work with directly.Typically, this is a professor that they have worked with in a class or faculty member with shared interests.
ANTH 451 and ANTH 453 are six-unit field school courses in which the student gains hands-on experience in research and study in the field under the direction of a faculty member.
Anthropology majors are limited to having no more than six credit hours of field-oriented coursework (ANTH 393, ANTH 395, ANTH 451, or ANTH 453) count toward meeting the major requirement, although they are not restricted from enrolling in more than six credit hours of these courses combined.

## Special Opportunities in Anthropology
### Study Abroad
Anthropology majors are encouraged to enroll in a study abroad program. These programs can offer direct experience of another culture and intensive language training, as well as excellent coursework in anthropology. By consulting with their departmental advisors as well as with the University’s Study Abroad Office, students can assess the relevance of available programs to their interests and arrange to transfer credit hours to count toward their undergraduate degree and, where appropriate, the anthropology major. Study abroad programs are often affordable even to students who require financial aid. Information about student loans and scholarships for the purpose of studying abroad can be obtained from the Study Abroad Office.

## Special Opportunities in Anthropology
### Undergraduate Awards
The Honigmann Undergraduate Honors Thesis Award is given each year to the student who completed the best undergraduate honors project.

**Grading Status:**Letter grade.

Survey of international social, political, and cultural patterns in selected societies of Africa, Asia, America, and Europe, stressing comparative analysis of conflicts and change in different historical contexts. LAC recitation sections offered in French, German, and Spanish.

Anthropology majors are limited to having no more than six credit hours of field-oriented coursework (ANTH 393, ANTH 395, ANTH 451, or ANTH 453) count toward meeting the major requirement, although they are not restricted from enrolling in more than six credit hours of these courses combined.

## Special Opportunities in Anthropology
### Study Abroad
Anthropology majors are encouraged to enroll in a study abroad program. These programs can offer direct experience of another culture and intensive language training, as well as excellent coursework in anthropology. By consulting with their departmental advisors as well as with the University’s Study Abroad Office, students can assess the relevance of available programs to their interests and arrange to transfer credit hours to count toward their undergraduate degree and, where appropriate, the anthropology major. Study abroad programs are often affordable even to students who require financial aid. Medical anthropology addresses the biological, cultural, and political-economic dimensions of health, illness, and healing historically and at present. Reflecting the multi-disciplinary character of its parent field of anthropology, medical anthropology deploys quantitative and qualitative methods to examine the body as a site of evolutionary processes and cultural symbols. Medical anthropology considers healing as a set of interpretive processes occurring at multiple, complex levels.
This program provides students with the fundamental knowledge and exposure needed to pursue careers and post-graduate studies in fields related to global health, public health, allied health care, health and human services, health policy, medicine, dentistry, and other emerging disciplines.
For students seeking a career in the health professions, the program in medical anthropology complements training in the natural sciences. Courses in medical anthropology explore population variations in health outcomes due to the influence of environment, context, and culture. The curriculum also equips students with ways to understand the meanings people find in illness and healing as well as the moral stakes of medical decisions. Additionally, courses in medical anthropology give students awareness of the formal institutions and social relations that become the channels and limitations of technical knowledge about illness and healing.

## Student Learning Outcomes
Upon completion of the medical anthropology program, students should be able to:
*   Demonstrate knowledge of the relationships between humans' health and historical, biocultural, and societal dynamics  
*   Demonstrate understanding of the ways comparative cultural and historical experiences impact health-related values and practices, definitions of illness, and methods of healing  
*   Demonstrate competence in reading, analyzing, and communicating social science research on health  
*   Gain experience conducting and/or applying research using medical anthropology's methods  
*   Gain an understanding of medical anthropology's relationships to the holistic, parent discipline of anthropology and its contributions to applied professional fields such as medicine and global health.

#### Lower-Division Courses
##### ANT X01. Biological Anthropology.
Introduction to the principles and the methods of biological (physical) anthropology. Overview of the study of human beings in an evolutionary context, our relationship to other primates, and to the rest of the natural world. Examines anatomical, behavioral, and genetic similarities and differences among living primates and basic mechanisms of the evolutionary process.

##### ANT X02. Cultural Anthropology.
The concept of culture; social and political organization; language; the supernatural; elementary cultural theory.

##### ANT X02H. Cultural Anthropology: Honors.
Explore the concept of culture, social and political organization, language, the supernatural, and elementary cultural theory.

##### ANT X04. Introduction to Archaeological Studies: Prehistoric Archaeology.
Anthropological study of prehistory, from human beginnings to the appearance of written records.

##### ANT X04T. Introduction to Texas Archaeology.
Introduces students to Texas archaeology through lectures, interactive virtual labs, and hands-on laboratory sections that emphasize experimentation.

##### ANT X05. Expressive Culture.
How cultural assumptions affect how we tell and respond to different kinds of stories, including fairy tales, movies, and televised news.

#### Lower-Division Courses
##### ANT X07. Culture and Communication.
An introduction to the study of culture through communication and the theory of signs.

#### Lower-Division Courses
##### ANT X10C. Primate Cognition.
Introduction to non-human primate knowledge of the physical world, as well as primate social knowledge. Examines non- human primate cognition within an evolutionary and comparative framework, with emphasis placed on comparing and contrasting non-human primate cognition with that of humans and other taxonomic groups.

#### Lower-Division Courses
##### ANT X10D. Introduction to Black Studies.
Introduction to canonical black studies literature, themes, and theories.

#### Lower-Division Courses
##### ANT X10F. African Diaspora Archaeology.


#### Lower-Division Courses
##### ANT X10G. Ethics of Space Exploration.
Examine cultural and ethical questions related to the exploration of space and the emerging field of astrobiology.

#### Lower-Division Courses
##### ANT X10I. Early Mesoamerican Religions.
Introduction to the study of indigenous religions in Mesoamerica, a geographic and cultural area spanning north-central Mexico through western Honduras, from approximately 250 BC - AD 1700. Examine the role of religion and ritual in daily life, as well as the lines of evidence available today for understanding them.

#### Lower-Division Courses
##### ANT X10J. The New Latinas/os/xs.
Explore the trajectories of various communities many have called the new Latinas/os/xs by identifying how race, gender, sexuality, class, indigeneity, language, migration, and geography influence the lives, identities, and sociopolitical incorporation of new Latinas/os/xs.

#### Lower-Division Courses
##### ANT X10L. Introductory Topics in Anthropology.

#### Lower-Division Courses
##### ANT X10L.3. Anthropology of Latin America.
Provides a framework for understanding contemporary concerns in Latin America.

#### Lower-Division Courses
##### ANT X10L.5. Introduction to South Asia.
Introduction to Indian and south Asian civilization, past and present, including religion, literature, arts, philosophy, and history.

Exploration of over two decades of work produced by and about black queer subjects throughout the circum-Atlantic world. Provides an introduction to various artists and intellectuals of the black queer diaspora, as well as an examination of the viability of black queer aesthetic practice as a form of theorizing.

##### ANT X10L.7. Diaspora: Race, Nation, and Resistance.
Subjects include makings and meanings of diaspora, the differences and similarities between diaspora and related concepts such as race, nation, and cultural identity. Focuses on the making of the black Atlantic world, and comparative analysis between black diasporic life and that of other global dispersals, particularly among Asian and indigenous populations, and how resistance serves as a key link.

##### ANT X10M. Mexican American and Latina/o Folkore Across the United States.

##### ANT X10R. Race, Sex, and Tourism.

##### ANT X11D. Introduction to Jewish Studies.

Historical and cultural analysis of how Jews constructed lives and communities in predominantly Hispanic, Catholic countries of Latin America.

Introduction to ancient Mesoamerica from the time of emerging social inequality in the formative period until the Spanish conquest of Mexico-Tenochtitlan in the sixteenth century.

Mexican American cultural distinctiveness in the areas of social organization, child rearing, food culture, folklore, language, and religion.

Explore the myriad of indigenous languages of North America and how they are intertwined with culture.

Examine speech play and verbal art (from puns to lies to songs to stories to poetry) from ethnographic and linguistic perspectives in a host of contexts and languages.

Examine invented languages from pidgin and creole languages to Esperanto or Basic English, and contemporary "conlangs" associated with various science fiction and fantasy series.

Examine the place of language in a variety of different political settings--from oblique oratory in small-scale egalitarian communities to ritual "poetry" in cosmic polities to procedural prose in mass bureaucratic states--to illustrate the power of words. Identify the varied ways language sustains and transforms power relations in different political contexts, and thereby takes on a power of its own. Examine language rights as a tool for defending small-scale and minority language communities against the spread of national and global languages.

##### ANT X20I. Talk, Text, and God.
Introduction to the anthropological study of Christianity, particularly in colonial and post-colonial settings.

#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X20O. New Media and Communication.
Explore anthropological and media studies analyses of technological changes in communications from the nineteenth through the twenty-first centuries.

#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X20P. Classical Archaeology: Practice and Ethics.
Explore an overview of the history, methods, approaches, and ethics of classical archaeology focusing on case studies of major sites and their excavations.

##### ANT X21C. Communicating with Non-Humans.
Examine the continuities and transformations in how people have tried to talk to nonhumans in different cultural contexts, whether those be gods, animals, the dead, or machines.

Examine how linguistic practices of (im)politeness and verbal aggression shape--and are shaped by--social hierarchies, cultural contexts, and political dynamics across different contexts, from liberal to anti-liberal. ##### ANT X22C. Contemporary African Popular Culture.

Aims to understand North Korea's historical development and its current workings as a social, cultural, and political/ideological system.

Examines critical spatial theory, landscape phenomenology, histories of Zionist architecture and urban planning as applied to Israel from the Yishuv period to the present.

Historical and cross-cultural overview of the relationship between feminine and religious cultural expressions through comparative examinations and analyses of various goddess figures in world religions.

History of major doctrines, practices, and institutions that shaped the development of Hinduism; how religions adapt to social and cultural change and often provide the catalyst for change.

#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X22O. Gender, Sexuality, and the Family in Indian Religions and Cultures.
A comprehensive historical overview of gender issues as they are represented in the textual traditions of South Asia.

Examines the history of Mexican immigration to the United States, and provides an overview of migratory patterns dating back to the late prehistoric period through contemporary times.

##### ANT X22Q. Mexican American Indigenous Heritage.
The prehistory, history, and contemporary racial understanding of Mexican Americans.

Examination of the Russian folktale, its roots in ancient, pre-Christian Slavic religious tradition, its connections with other forms of folklore such as myth and legend, and its transformation in modern Russian literature. Use the tools of cultural anthropology to understand the touristic encounter and the increasing (and decreasing) accessibility of travel and mobility.

#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X22V. Architecture and Sculpture in the Maya World.
Explore the ancient world of the Maya through the lens of architecture and sculpture.

##### ANT X22W. Power and Resistance in Putin's Russia.
Introduction to Russian political and protest cultures--beyond the headlines and outside the Kremlin walls.

##### ANT X23C. Sport, Religion, and Society.
Explore sport as it relates to ritual and religious practice and examine the meaning and nature of sport in cross-cultural perspectives.

Examine the histories and politics of religious practices in the Greater Caribbean, encompassing the islands and Central American coasts as well as the continental diasporas, from Vodou and Rastafari to popular Hinduism.

Consider the power struggles of the democratic process by closely attending to language, rhetoric and performance.

Explore what life is like in today's contested, rapidly growing, and increasingly diverse Jerusalem.

Explore how infrastructure creates relationships between resources, energy, built form, information, and people.

Explore a sensory ethnographic investigation of urban ecology, organized around air, water, earth, and fire as themes for engaging with the city through media and the senses.

Historical and cross-cultural overview of the constructed concepts of magic, science, and religion through comparative examinations of cultural contexts from the Islamic world, western Europe, the Caribbean, the U.S., and Mozambique.

##### ANT X24J. HIV and AIDS Activism and the Healing Arts.

Course material will draw from film, literature, history, geography, and anthropology.

#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X24L.48. Sex and Power in the African Diaspora.
Exploration of various experiences and theories of sex, intimacy, and desire alongside intellectual and artistic engagements with power hierarchies and spirituality across transnational black communities. Subjects include the concept of "erotic subjectivity" from various theoretical and methodological angles, principally within African diasporic contexts.

#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X24L.49. Global Markets and Local Cultures.
Examine contemporary theories of globalization, including materials exploring global governance, international monetary policy, migration regulation, offshoring, and cultural hybridity. Focus on case studies in Asia and elsewhere that reveal how these practices impact particular communities.

#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X24L.51. The Cities of the Middle East.
Anthropological and sociological analysis of space, with a special emphasis on urban theory and culture in the Middle East.

#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X24L.53. Global Indigenous Issues.
Explores contemporary issues of indigenous peoples around the world through films, literature, and social science readings and focuses on how indigenous peoples are actively working to oppose their oppression and create sustainable futures.

#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X24L.54. Black Native American Relations in the United States.
Explores the entwined histories, cultures, and identities of African American and Native American people in North America. Subjects include experiences of racial formation, including how race, power, and indigeneity work in different ways for people in contemporary United States society.

#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X24L.56. Ethnographic Writing.
Writing workshop consisting of a series of exercises to add density and texture to ethnographic description by including attention to scene, character, event, situation, and dialogue.

#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X24L.57. Archaeology of Climate Change.
Examines why climate changes, the methods for recording climate change, and includes case studies of the varied responses of past human societies to climate change in different geographic regions and time periods with varying socio-political and economic systems.

#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X24L.58. Digital Data Systems in Archaeology.
Designed to help students understand the basic knowledge and skills needed to operate digital equipment (e.g. GPS and Total Data Stations) commonly used for collecting location data on archaeological sites. Instruction on mapping and grid systems translates into "hands-on instrument operation in simulated archaeological field conditions. Provides an introduction to GIS software and its applications in archaeology as well as an overview of near-surface sensing techniques.

#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X24L.59. Graffiti and Poster Art in the Islamic World.


#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X24L.63. Food and Culture.
Examines cultural and linguistic views on eating and how we talk about what we eat in the contemporary era. Combines scholarly literature, videos, and readings about food subjects that circulate in popular culture, and considers how flows of dietary images and discourses shape race/ethnicity, gender, social class, and other identifications.

#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X24L.64. The Bronze Age and the Iron Age in Atlantic Europe.
Introduction to the archaeology of Atlantic Europe with particular emphasis on the Bronze Age and Iron Age periods. Examines the diversity and commonalities of European adaptations, investigates how geography influenced trade of goods and ideas, as well as the profound changes brought about by a new conceptualization of the world and the innovations of the Bronze and Iron Ages.

#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X24L.65. Anthropology for Liberation.
Takes a critical look at anthropologists' quests to shifting the legacy of anthropology from the colonial toward freedom and liberation. Explores anthropology's relationship to human rights, violence, questions of race, gender, and sexuality, imperialism and neoliberalism, and the ways that some anthropologists have chosen to use their field work in new and different ways.

#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X24L.66. Indigenizing Queer Theory.
Introduction to emerging work by indigenous queer theorists, largely from the United States. Examines cultural conflicts between the west and indigenous world views and practices surrounding monogamy and marriage, same-sex marriage, enforced gender binaries, sexual identities and practices, their regulation by the colonial state, and implications for indigenous people.

#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X24L.68. Creation and Evolution: Human Origins in Scientific and Religious Discourses.
Examines evolutionary theory, intelligent design, and creationism, and how they interact.

#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X24L.69. Japanese Concepts of Body and Self.
Exploration of anthropological literature describing Japanese conceptions of self and body, and analysis of the intersection of these conceptions of self with Japanese ideas about religion, morality, aging, and medicine.

#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X24L.7. Introduction to African Prehistory.


#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X24L.71. Extraterrestrial Intelligence: Culture, Religion, and Imagination.
Focusing primarily on the 20th and 21st Centuries, explores the search for extraterrestrial intelligence (SETI) and considers how these ideas have intersected with other aspects of society, particularly religion, including recent arguments that SETI itself has developed into a religion. Examines meanings and motivations behind issues such as Percival Lowell's quest to prove the existence of canals on Mars and the development of Scientology.

#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X24L.72. Development, Security, and Society.
Explores the linkages between development, security, and, society. Examines a series of recent transformations that have drawn the relationship between international development and various forms of security together. Through an exploration of recent anthropological work, examines subjects such as: human security, the relationship between development and humanitarian intervention, strategies for planning in the face of climate change, disaster management, and new technologies of warfare and security.

#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X24L.73. Political Ecology.
Introduction to core tenets of political ecology. Focuses on ethnographic approaches and introduces key debates in the field--such as the relationship between environment and violence, the critique of Malthusian and neo-Malthusian notions of scarcity and limits, the links between conservation and dispossession, and more. Explores the uses of political ecology in key contemporary debates over social and environmental change, from climate change to waste management.

#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X24L.74. Inca World.
Explores how Inca civilization developed, how the Incas grew from a small highland state into a mighty empire, and how a small number of Spaniards and their allies were able to bring the Inca dynasty to an end. Read accounts of the Incas written in the first years of Spanish colonial rule, and review the latest archaeological discoveries.

#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X24L.75. Arab Latin Americas.
Examine the ways in which Arab immigrant identities have been negotiated and co-opted socially, but also institutionally, in various countries in the Western Hemisphere.

#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X24L.76. Indigenous Peoples of Russia and the USSR.
Examine an introduction to theories of colonial critique and visual culture studies. Explore the history of the Indigenous peoples of the Eurasian north.

#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X24L.77. Blacks and Asians: Race and Social Movements.
Examines the relations between Asians and Blacks in the United States.

#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X24L.78. Black Women and the State.
Surveys black women's experiences living with and confronting state oppression around the world. Takes an historical, social, and theoretical look at the roots of this oppression and inequality, and how black women have chosen to respond to it locally and globally.

#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X24L.8. Cultures of Southeast Asia.
Comparative study of the peoples of Indonesia, Burma, Thailand, Malaysia, and other countries.

#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X24L.9. The African Diaspora in the Americas.
Black cultures and societies in the New World, and their African heritage.

#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X24N. Muslim Women in Politics.


#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X24O. Globalization in Latin America.
Critically examine the globalization phenomenon in Latin America, focusing on history and ethnography.

#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X24P. Gender and Labor in Global Asia.


#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X24Q. Global Perspectives of Health, Illness, and Inequality.
Use an anthropological framework to think critically and analytically about global past and contemporary issues in health. Examine the root causes of health, illness, and inequality.

#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X24R. Daily Life in Mesoamerica.
Examine the daily life of people in Mesoamerica, from the earliest inhabitants in the region to the myriad ways that Precolumbian life and archaeology affect the lives of people today.

#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X24S. The Global City.


#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X24U. Socialism's Past and Futures.
Examine ordinary people's experience of socialism in the Soviet Union and the plural interpretations of this experience after the USSR's collapse.

#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X24V. Sexuality in Global Perspective.
Explore the ways in which sexuality intersects with money, intimacy, power, and labor in the context of global economic processes.

#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X24W. Mapping Indigenous Austin.
Explore the histories and presence of indigenous Austin.

#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X25C. Cultures of Sustainability.
Examine how ecological concerns are articulated and perceived in different cultural contexts.

#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X25D. Representation of Jews in the American Public Sphere.
Examines how Jews have been represented and constituted in American public culture as a race, religion, and/or nation through distinct institutions and display practices.

#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X25E. Ethnographies of Emotion.
Examine concepts such as place, character, objects, subjects, cultural forms, everyday life, and feeling states or structures such as trauma, love, hope, depression, the even keel, and melodrama through a writing workshop. Explore how to articulate structures of feeling with models of culture and the self. Analyze and experiment with modes of ethnographic attention, the importance of telling detail, and methods of participant observation.

#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X25F. Cultural Heritage on Display.
Explore the public construction and display of traditional American folk culture by studying popular folklife-oriented tourist sites.

#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X25G. Technoculture.
Analyze social groups using digital methods and a process of self-reflection focused on technological mediations of experience.

#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X25I. Sonic Ethnography.
Examine sound, themes of listening, noise, silence, audio technology, vibration, and voice.

#### Lower-Division Courses
##### ANT X01. Biological Anthropology.
Introduction to the principles and the methods of biological (physical) anthropology. Overview of the study of human beings in an evolutionary context, our relationship to other primates, and to the rest of the natural world. Examines anatomical, behavioral, and genetic similarities and differences among living primates and basic mechanisms of the evolutionary process.
texts.1:

##### ANT X02. Cultural Anthropology.
The concept of culture; social and political organization; language; the supernatural; elementary cultural theory.
texts.2:
#### Lower-Division Courses
##### ANT X02H. Cultural Anthropology: Honors.
Explore the concept of culture, social and political organization, language, the supernatural, and elementary cultural theory.
texts.3:
#### Lower-Division Courses
##### ANT X04. Introduction to Archaeological Studies: Prehistoric Archaeology.
Anthropological study of prehistory, from human beginnings to the appearance of written records.
texts.4:
#### Lower-Division Courses
##### ANT X04T. Introduction to Texas Archaeology.
Introduces students to Texas archaeology through lectures, interactive virtual labs, and hands-on laboratory sections that emphasize experimentation.
texts.5:
#### Lower-Division Courses
##### ANT X05. Expressive Culture.
How cultural assumptions affect how we tell and respond to different kinds of stories, including fairy tales, movies, and televised news.
texts.6:
#### Lower-Division Courses
##### ANT X07. Culture and Communication.
An introduction to the study of culture through communication and the theory of signs.
texts.7:
#### Lower-Division Courses
##### ANT X10C. Primate Cognition.
Introduction to non-human primate knowledge of the physical world, as well as primate social knowledge. Examines non- human primate cognition within an evolutionary and comparative framework, with emphasis placed on comparing and contrasting non-human primate cognition with that of humans and other taxonomic groups.
texts.8:
#### Lower-Division Courses
##### ANT X10D. Introduction to Black Studies.
Introduction to canonical black studies literature, themes, and theories.
texts.9:
#### Lower-Division Courses
##### ANT X10F. African Diaspora Archaeology.
texts.10:
#### Lower-Division Courses
##### ANT X10G. Ethics of Space Exploration.
Examine cultural and ethical questions related to the exploration of space and the emerging field of astrobiology.
texts.11:
#### Lower-Division Courses
##### ANT X10I. Early Mesoamerican Religions.
Introduction to the study of indigenous religions in Mesoamerica, a geographic and cultural area spanning north-central Mexico through western Honduras, from approximately 250 BC - AD 1700. Examine the role of religion and ritual in daily life, as well as the lines of evidence available today for understanding them.
texts.12:
#### Lower-Division Courses
##### ANT X10J. The New Latinas/os/xs.
Explore the trajectories of various communities many have called the new Latinas/os/xs by identifying how race, gender, sexuality, class, indigeneity, language, migration, and geography influence the lives, identities, and sociopolitical incorporation of new Latinas/os/xs.
texts.13:
#### Lower-Division Courses
##### ANT X10L. Introductory Topics in Anthropology.
texts.14:
#### Lower-Division Courses
##### ANT X10L.2. Anthropology of Race and Ethnicity: An Introduction.
Examines the social importance of race and ethnicity both in America and around the world.
texts.15:
#### Lower-Division Courses
##### ANT X10L.3. Anthropology of Latin America.
Provides a framework for understanding contemporary concerns in Latin America.
texts.16:
#### Lower-Division Courses
##### ANT X10L.5. Introduction to South Asia.
Introduction to Indian and south Asian civilization, past and present, including religion, literature, arts, philosophy, and history.
texts.17:
#### Lower-Division Courses
##### ANT X10L.6. Black Queer Art Worlds.
Exploration of over two decades of work produced by and about black queer subjects throughout the circum-Atlantic world. Provides an introduction to various artists and intellectuals of the black queer diaspora, as well as an examination of the viability of black queer aesthetic practice as a form of theorizing.
texts.18:
#### Lower-Division Courses
##### ANT X10L.7. Diaspora: Race, Nation, and Resistance.
Subjects include makings and meanings of diaspora, the differences and similarities between diaspora and related concepts such as race, nation, and cultural identity. Focuses on the making of the black Atlantic world, and comparative analysis between black diasporic life and that of other global dispersals, particularly among Asian and indigenous populations, and how resistance serves as a key link.
texts.19:
#### Lower-Division Courses
##### ANT X10M. Mexican American and Latina/o Folkore Across the United States.
texts.20:
#### Lower-Division Courses
##### ANT X10R. Race, Sex, and Tourism.
texts.21:
#### Lower-Division Courses
##### ANT X11D. Introduction to Jewish Studies.
texts.22:
#### Lower-Division Courses
##### ANT X11E. Introduction to Jewish Latin America.
Historical and cultural analysis of how Jews constructed lives and communities in predominantly Hispanic, Catholic countries of Latin America.
texts.23:
#### Lower-Division Courses
##### ANT X14C. Introduction to Mesoamerican Archaeology.
Introduction to ancient Mesoamerica from the time of emerging social inequality in the formative period until the Spanish conquest of Mexico-Tenochtitlan in the sixteenth century.
texts.24:
#### Lower-Division Courses
##### ANT X18L. Mexican American Culture.
Mexican American cultural distinctiveness in the areas of social organization, child rearing, food culture, folklore, language, and religion.

##### ANT X19S. Topics in Anthropology.
This course is used to record credit the student earns while enrolled at another institution in a program administered by the University's Study Abroad Office. Credit is recorded as assigned by the study abroad adviser in the Department of Anthropology. University credit is awarded for work in an exchange program; it may be counted as coursework taken in residence. Transfer credit is awarded for work in an affiliated studies program.

##### ANT X29S. Topics in Anthropology.
This course is used to record credit the student earns while enrolled at another institution in a program administered by the University's Study Abroad Office. Credit is recorded as assigned by the study abroad adviser in the Department of Anthropology. University credit is awarded for work in an exchange program; it may be counted as coursework taken in residence. Transfer credit is awarded for work in an affiliated studies program.
texts.27:
#### Lower-Division Courses
##### ANT X76P. Research Internship.
Supervised fieldwork in a business or community setting related to the student's career and research interests. Students conduct research and apply anthropological skills to real-world problems.
texts.28:
#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X19S. Topics in Anthropology.
This course is used to record credit the student earns while enrolled at another institution in a program administered by the University's Study Abroad Office. Credit is recorded as assigned by the study abroad adviser in the Department of Anthropology. University credit is awarded for work in an exchange program; it may be counted as coursework taken in residence. Transfer credit is awarded for work in an affiliated studies program.
texts.29:
#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X20C. American Indian Languages and Cultures.
Explore the myriad of indigenous languages of North America and how they are intertwined with culture.
texts.30:
#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X20D. Speech Play and Verbal Art.
Examine speech play and verbal art (from puns to lies to songs to stories to poetry) from ethnographic and linguistic perspectives in a host of contexts and languages.
texts.31:
#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X20E. Invented Languages.
Examine invented languages from pidgin and creole languages to Esperanto or Basic English, and contemporary "conlangs" associated with various science fiction and fantasy series.
texts.32:
#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X20F. Politics, Polity, and the Power of Words.
Examine the place of language in a variety of different political settings--from oblique oratory in small-scale egalitarian communities to ritual "poetry" in cosmic polities to procedural prose in mass bureaucratic states--to illustrate the power of words. Identify the varied ways language sustains and transforms power relations in different political contexts, and thereby takes on a power of its own. Explore a variety of political situations, different modes of political communication, as well as different theories of the "performative" power of words.
texts.33:
#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X20G. Endangered Languages.
Examine language rights as a tool for defending small-scale and minority language communities against the spread of national and global languages.
texts.34:
#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X20I. Talk, Text, and God.
Introduction to the anthropological study of Christianity, particularly in colonial and post-colonial settings.
texts.35:
#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X20O. New Media and Communication.
Explore anthropological and media studies analyses of technological changes in communications from the nineteenth through the twenty-first centuries.
texts.36:
#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X20P. Classical Archaeology: Practice and Ethics.
Explore an overview of the history, methods, approaches, and ethics of classical archaeology focusing on case studies of major sites and their excavations.
texts.37:
#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X21C. Communicating with Non-Humans.
Examine the continuities and transformations in how people have tried to talk to nonhumans in different cultural contexts, whether those be gods, animals, the dead, or machines.
texts.38:
#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X21P. The Politics of Insult.
Examine how linguistic practices of (im)politeness and verbal aggression shape--and are shaped by--social hierarchies, cultural contexts, and political dynamics across different contexts, from liberal to anti-liberal. Analyze how seemingly neutral concepts of "civility" and appropriate speech" often mask power relations while exploring how taboo language, conflict talk, and transgressive communication can both challenge and reinforce existing social orders.
texts.39:
#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X22C. Contemporary African Popular Culture.
texts.40:
#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X22D. Multicultural Israel.
Examines the complex social fabric that comprises contemporary Israeli society, and that shapes Israeli identity, practice and politics.
texts.41:
#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X22E. Self and Culture in North Korea.
Aims to understand North Korea's historical development and its current workings as a social, cultural, and political/ideological system.
texts.42:
#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X22F. Big Asian Histories.
Examines ways in which Asia and other areas of the globe have had connected intellectual, artistic, and social developments with focus on world histories centrally involving Asia from the medieval period to the present.
texts.43:
#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X22G. Cultural Geographies of Israel.
Examines critical spatial theory, landscape phenomenology, histories of Zionist architecture and urban planning as applied to Israel from the Yishuv period to the present.
texts.44:
#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X22I. Native American Cultures of the Southwest.
Explore the diverse Native cultures of the Southwest, focusing on the philosophical underpinnings and the frameworks of meaning and moral responsibility of indigenous peoples of the American Southwest.
texts.45:
#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X22J. Goddesses in World Religions and Cultures.
Historical and cross-cultural overview of the relationship between feminine and religious cultural expressions through comparative examinations and analyses of various goddess figures in world religions.
texts.46:
#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X22N. History of Hindu Religious Traditions.
History of major doctrines, practices, and institutions that shaped the development of Hinduism; how religions adapt to social and cultural change and often provide the catalyst for change.
texts.47:
#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X22O. Gender, Sexuality, and the Family in Indian Religions and Cultures.
A comprehensive historical overview of gender issues as they are represented in the textual traditions of South Asia.
texts.48:
#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X22P. Mexican Immigration Cultural History.
Examines the history of Mexican immigration to the United States, and provides an overview of migratory patterns dating back to the late prehistoric period through contemporary times.
texts.49:
#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X22Q. Mexican American Indigenous Heritage.
The prehistory, history, and contemporary racial understanding of Mexican Americans.
texts.50:
#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X22T. Russian Myths and Folktales.
Examination of the Russian folktale, its roots in ancient, pre-Christian Slavic religious tradition, its connections with other forms of folklore such as myth and legend, and its transformation in modern Russian literature. Subjects include the continuing influence of folklore explored through various aspects of Russian culture, including literature, music, ballet, film, and popular culture.
texts.51:
#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X22U. Anthropology of Travel and Tourism.
Use the tools of cultural anthropology to understand the touristic encounter and the increasing (and decreasing) accessibility of travel and mobility.
texts.52:
#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X22V. Architecture and Sculpture in the Maya World.
Explore the ancient world of the Maya through the lens of architecture and sculpture.
texts.53:
#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X22W. Power and Resistance in Putin's Russia.
Introduction to Russian political and protest cultures--beyond the headlines and outside the Kremlin walls.
texts.54:
#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X23C. Sport, Religion, and Society.
Explore sport as it relates to ritual and religious practice and examine the meaning and nature of sport in cross-cultural perspectives.
texts.55:
#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X23D. Religions of the Caribbean.
Examine the histories and politics of religious practices in the Greater Caribbean, encompassing the islands and Central American coasts as well as the continental diasporas, from Vodou and Rastafari to popular Hinduism.
texts.56:
#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X23E. Politics and Performance.
Consider the power struggles of the democratic process by closely attending to language, rhetoric and performance.
texts.57:
#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X23I. Comparative White Nationalisms.
Consider critical questions about the constructions of whiteness and nationalism across the globe. Examine, through an anthropological lens, how the boundaries of whiteness changed throughout history, and its relationship to far-right political groups, to trace the history of white nationalism and its present-day global resurgence.
texts.58:
#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X23N. Biomedicine, Ethics, and Culture.
Examines ethical questions such as the allocation of medical resources, stem cell research and cloning, organ transplantation, abortion, human experimentation, prolonging life and the right to die, suicide, euthanasia, and diagnosis and treatment of illnesses, explored from a global perspective.
texts.59:
#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X23O. Black Geographies.
Explore the relationship between Blackness and the production of space and place. Examine the tensions and possibilities that emerge when Black people are rendered un-geographic as a fundamental component of racial capitalism while they are simultaneously creating spaces of freedom under constant threats to Black life.
texts.60:
#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X23P. Anthropology of the Himalayas.
Examine the history and culture of the Himalayan region, including Northeast India, sections of Pakistan and Afghanistan, Tibet, and especially Nepal.
texts.61:
#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X23Q. Contemporary Jerusalem.
Explore what life is like in today's contested, rapidly growing, and increasingly diverse Jerusalem.
texts.62:
#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X23R. Anthropology of Infrastructure.
Explore how infrastructure creates relationships between resources, energy, built form, information, and people.
texts.63:
#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X23S. Anthropology of Food.
Explore the cultural dimensions of growing, cooking, and eating food by engaging themes of gender, race, indigeneity, embodiment, hunger, and power.
texts.64:
#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X23T. Colonial Encounters in Mesoamerica.
Study European-indigenous encounters in Mesoamerica, a geographic and cultural area spanning north-central Mexico through western Honduras, between approximately 1450-1750. Examine strategies of contact, accommodation, and resistance that indigenous communities and European colonizers used to communicate with each other and negotiate the conduct of daily life in colonial society.
texts.65:
#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X23U. Sensing: Elemental Media.
Explore a sensory ethnographic investigation of urban ecology, organized around air, water, earth, and fire as themes for engaging with the city through media and the senses.
texts.66:
#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X23V. Maya Art and Architecture.
Introduction to the artistic traditions of the ancient Maya, tracing their development up to the time of European contact. Students will examine various important themes of Maya culture including history, ritual, and cosmology as revealed in sculpture, hieroglyphs, painting, and architectural design.
texts.67:
#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X23W. Race and Indigeneity in the Pacific.
Examine a multidisciplinary study of sovereignty, settler colonialism, diaspora, and migration in the Pacific.
texts.68:
#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X24C. Science, Magic, and Religion.
Historical and cross-cultural overview of the constructed concepts of magic, science, and religion through comparative examinations of cultural contexts from the Islamic world, western Europe, the Caribbean, the U.S., and Mozambique.
texts.69:
#### Upper-Division Courses
##### ANT X24D. Japanese Religion and Western Imagination.
Examines Japanese religious traditions, with a focus on Zen, through the perspective of people living in non-Japanese societies since the end of World War II. Explores different ways in which non-Japanese have imagined Japanese religious and ethical ideas and both explained Japanese behavior and adopted ideas about Japan into their writings about philosophy and life.

An exploration of the complex relationship between anthropological ideas and ethnographic practice. Introduces a broad spectrum of concepts, issues, and theories of culture, and critically examines how these theories and ideas shape anthropological methods and writings.

Anthropological analysis of gender and sexuality that critically evaluates formative concepts and theories that have been subject to recent debates within anthropology, gender studies, and queer theory.

Analysis of the roots of urban unrest, exploring a range of origins: joblessness, state violence, white flight, backlash against civil rights gains, new immigration, and interracial strife. Beyond race and class, subjects include exploring unrest as a mode of pushing the normative boundaries of gender and sexuality in public space. Course material will draw from film, literature, history, geography, and anthropology.

Exploration of various experiences and theories of sex, intimacy, and desire alongside intellectual and artistic engagements with power hierarchies and spirituality across transnational black communities. Subjects include the concept of "erotic subjectivity" from various theoretical and methodological angles, principally within African diasporic contexts.

Examine contemporary theories of globalization, including materials exploring global governance, international monetary policy, migration regulation, offshoring, and cultural hybridity. Focus on case studies in Asia and elsewhere that reveal how these practices impact particular communities.

Anthropological and sociological analysis of space, with a special emphasis on urban theory and culture in the Middle East.

Writing workshop consisting of a series of exercises to add density and texture to ethnographic description by including attention to scene, character, event, situation, and dialogue.

Examines why climate changes, the methods for recording climate change, and includes case studies of the varied responses of past human societies to climate change in different geographic regions and time periods with varying socio-political and economic systems.

##### ANT X24L.58. Digital Data Systems in Archaeology.
Designed to help students understand the basic knowledge and skills needed to operate digital equipment (e.g. GPS and Total Data Stations) commonly used for collecting location data on archaeological sites. Instruction on mapping and grid systems translates into "hands-on instrument operation in simulated archaeological field conditions. Provides an introduction to GIS software and its applications in archaeology as well as an overview of near-surface sensing techniques.

Examines cultural and linguistic views on eating and how we talk about what we eat in the contemporary era. Combines scholarly literature, videos, and readings about food subjects that circulate in popular culture, and considers how flows of dietary images and discourses shape race/ethnicity, gender, social class, and other identifications.

##### ANT X24L.64. The Bronze Age and the Iron Age in Atlantic Europe.
Introduction to the archaeology of Atlantic Europe with particular emphasis on the Bronze Age and Iron Age periods. Examines the diversity and commonalities of European adaptations, investigates how geography influenced trade of goods and ideas, as well as the profound changes brought about by a new conceptualization of the world and the innovations of the Bronze and Iron Ages.

##### ANT X24L.65. Anthropology for Liberation.
Takes a critical look at anthropologists' quests to shifting the legacy of anthropology from the colonial toward freedom and liberation. Explores anthropology's relationship to human rights, violence, questions of race, gender, and sexuality, imperialism and neoliberalism, and the ways that some anthropologists have chosen to use their field work in new and different ways.

Introduction to emerging work by indigenous queer theorists, largely from the United States. Examines cultural conflicts between the west and indigenous world views and practices surrounding monogamy and marriage, same-sex marriage, enforced gender binaries, sexual identities and practices, their regulation by the colonial state, and implications for indigenous people.

Examines evolutionary theory, intelligent design, and creationism, and how they interact.

Exploration of anthropological literature describing Japanese conceptions of self and body, and analysis of the intersection of these conceptions of self with Japanese ideas about religion, morality, aging, and medicine.

Focusing primarily on the 20th and 21st Centuries, explores the search for extraterrestrial intelligence (SETI) and considers how these ideas have intersected with other aspects of society, particularly religion, including recent arguments that SETI itself has developed into a religion. Examines meanings and motivations behind issues such as Percival Lowell's quest to prove the existence of canals on Mars and the development of Scientology.

Explores the linkages between development, security, and, society. Examines a series of recent transformations that have drawn the relationship between international development and various forms of security together. Through an exploration of recent anthropological work, examines subjects such as: human security, the relationship between development and humanitarian intervention, strategies for planning in the face of climate change, disaster management, and new technologies of warfare and security.

Introduction to core tenets of political ecology. Focuses on ethnographic approaches and introduces key debates in the field--such as the relationship between environment and violence, the critique of Malthusian and neo-Malthusian notions of scarcity and limits, the links between conservation and dispossession, and more.
